Authority: Commission Nationale pour la Protection des Données (CNPD), Luxembourg
Target: Amazon Europe Core S.à.r.l.
Decision Date: 2021-07-16
Fine Amount: EUR 746,000,000
Fine Category: GDPR Tier 2 (Art 83(5))

Violations:
- GDPR Article 6(1) — processing personal data for targeted advertising without valid legal basis
- GDPR Articles 12-14 — insufficient transparency about advertising data processing

Facts:
Following a 2018 complaint co-ordinated by La Quadrature du Net (a French digital rights NGO), the Luxembourg DPA investigated Amazon's targeted advertising system. Amazon processed customer behavioural data for ad targeting without obtaining valid consent and without adequate transparency about how the system worked. The complaint was filed under GDPR Article 80(1) on behalf of over 10,000 individuals.

Key Findings:
1. Amazon's advertising targeting system processed personal data without valid consent
2. Cookie consent mechanisms did not meet GDPR requirements
3. Behavioural profiling for advertising purposes lacked a valid legal basis
4. Amazon's privacy policy was insufficiently transparent about the ad targeting system
5. The fine was calculated based on Amazon's EUR 44 billion EU revenue (c. 1.7%)

Corrective Measures:
- Bring advertising data processing into compliance with GDPR consent requirements
- Overhaul cookie consent mechanisms

Appeal Status: Fine reduced to EUR 746M on appeal (confirmed 2024). Amazon reformed consent mechanisms.

- AI profiling for advertising must have an explicit, informed legal basis — not just 'legitimate interest'
- AI personalisation engines using behavioural data face the same consent and transparency requirements
- Revenue-based fine calculation means large AI companies face proportionally massive penalties

BA failed to detect the breach for over two months (June-September 2018).

Enhance payment card data handling procedures

Authority: Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), United Kingdom
Target: British Airways plc
Decision Date: 2020-10-16
Fine Amount: EUR 22,046,000 (GBP 20,000,000 — reduced from initial notice of GBP 183M)
Fine Category: GDPR Tier 2 (Art 83(5))

Violations:
- GDPR Article 5(1)(f) — failure to process data securely
- GDPR Article 32 — failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures

Facts:
In 2018, attackers exploited vulnerabilities in British Airways' website and mobile app by injecting malicious code (Magecart-style skimming attack) that redirected customer payment card details to an attacker-controlled server. Approximately 429,612 customers and staff members were affected. Data compromised included names, addresses, payment card numbers (including CVV codes), and login credentials. BA failed to detect the breach for over two months (June-September 2018).

Key Findings:
1. BA did not have adequate security testing or monitoring to detect the Magecart script injection
2. Multi-factor authentication was not implemented for key systems
3. Excessive storage of payment card data (including CVV codes) increased impact
4. BA failed to detect the breach for over 2 months despite available detection controls
5. The initial proposed fine of GBP 183M was reduced by 89% due to COVID-19 economic impact and BA's cooperation

Corrective Measures:
- Implement comprehensive security improvements including script monitoring
- Enhance payment card data handling procedures

Appeal Status: Fine reduced from GBP 183M to GBP 20M (no further appeal)

AI Relevance:
- AI-powered security monitoring (anomaly detection, intrusion detection) could have detected the breach earlier
- AI systems processing payment data must implement robust security measures under Art 32
- AI web applications face the same injection/skimming risks — security by design required
- AI-based fraud detection systems handling card data must meet the same standards

GDPRHub Facts Summary:
An ICO investigation found the airline was processing a significant amount of personal data without adequate security measures in place. This failure broke data protection law and, subsequently, British Airways (BA) was the subject of a cyber-attack during 2018, which it did not detect for more than two months. ICO investigators found BA ought to have identified weaknesses in its security and resolved them with security measures that were available at the time. The attacker is believed to have potentially accessed the personal data of approximately 429,612 customers and staff. This included names, addresses, payment card numbers and CVV numbers of 244,000 BA customers. Other details thought to have been accessed include the combined card and CVV numbers of 77,000 customers and card numbers only for 108,000 customers.

GDPRHub Holding Summary:
The ICO held that BA was indeed liable. Because the BA breach happened in June 2018, before the UK left the EU, the ICO investigated on behalf of all EU authorities as lead supervisory authority under the GDPR. There were numerous measures BA could have used to mitigate or prevent the risk of an attacker being able to access the BA network. None of these measures would have entailed excessive cost or technical barriers, with some available through the Microsoft Operating System used by BA. Therefore, considering this, the ICO found that BA had failed to comply with Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.

name: Clearview AI Biometric Fines
authority: Multiple DPAs: CNIL (France), Garante (Italy), ICO (UK), HDPA (Greece), AP (Netherlands)
facts: Clearview AI, a US-based company, scraped over 30 billion images from the internet (social media, news sites, public databases) to build a facial recognition database. The system extracts biometric templates (mathematical hashes) from facial images and sells search access to law enforcement and private companies. Multiple EU DPAs investigated following complaints and found that Clearview processed EU citizens' biometric data without any legal basis, failed to respond to access and erasure requests, and refused to cooperate with supervisory authorities.

Biometric templates derived from facial images are special category data under Art 9 GDPR
GDPR applies extraterritorially to Clearview AI under Art 3(2)(b) — monitoring of EU data subjects' behaviour
No legal basis exists for mass scraping of facial images for commercial purposes
Clearview's 'law enforcement use' argument rejected — commercial sale is the dominant purpose
UK ICO fine of GBP 7.5M was overturned on appeal (tribunal found processing was for law enforcement purposes outside GDPR scope)
Legitimate interest cannot justify biometric data processing at this scale
corrective_measures: Delete all biometric data of EU/EEA residents
Cease all scraping and processing of EU data subjects' biometric data
Appoint an EU representative
Comply with data subject access and erasure requests

Web scraping for AI training datasets must exclude biometric/sensitive data without legal basis
AI companies outside the EU face GDPR enforcement under extraterritorial provisions (Art 3(2))
AI biometric processing (face recognition, emotion detection, gait analysis) falls under Art 9 strict regime
Multiple coordinated EU DPA enforcement against a single AI company demonstrates regulatory convergence

Authority: Multiple DPAs: CNIL (France), Garante (Italy), ICO (UK), HDPA (Greece), AP (Netherlands)
Target: Clearview AI Inc.
Decision Date: 2022-2024 (multiple decisions)
Fine Amount: EUR 90,500,000+ combined (France: EUR 20M; Italy: EUR 20M; Greece: EUR 20M; Netherlands: EUR 30.5M; UK: GBP 7.5M overturned on appeal)
Fine Category: GDPR Tier 2 (Art 83(5))

Violations:
- GDPR Article 6(1) — no legal basis for scraping and processing biometric data
- GDPR Article 9 — unlawful processing of biometric data (special category)
- GDPR Article 12, 15, 17 — violation of data subject rights (access, erasure)
- GDPR Article 31 — failure to cooperate with DPAs
- GDPR Article 3(2) — extraterritorial application to US company monitoring EU individuals

Facts:
Clearview AI, a US-based company, scraped over 30 billion images from the internet (social media, news sites, public databases) to build a facial recognition database. The system extracts biometric templates (mathematical hashes) from facial images and sells search access to law enforcement and private companies. Multiple EU DPAs investigated following complaints and found that Clearview processed EU citizens' biometric data without any legal basis, failed to respond to access and erasure requests, and refused to cooperate with supervisory authorities.

Key Findings:
1. Web scraping of publicly available images for facial recognition constitutes unlawful processing of biometric data
2. Biometric templates derived from facial images are special category data under Art 9 GDPR
3. GDPR applies extraterritorially to Clearview AI under Art 3(2)(b) — monitoring of EU data subjects' behaviour
4. No legal basis exists for mass scraping of facial images for commercial purposes
5. Clearview's 'law enforcement use' argument rejected — commercial sale is the dominant purpose
6. UK ICO fine of GBP 7.5M was overturned on appeal (tribunal found processing was for law enforcement purposes outside GDPR scope)
7. Legitimate interest cannot justify biometric data processing at this scale

Corrective Measures:
- Delete all biometric data of EU/EEA residents
- Cease all scraping and processing of EU data subjects' biometric data
- Appoint an EU representative
- Comply with data subject access and erasure requests

Appeal Status: France, Italy, Greece, Netherlands fines stand. UK GBP 7.5M overturned (2023). Clearview largely non-compliant.

AI Relevance:
- AI facial recognition trained on scraped biometric data is UNLAWFUL under GDPR without explicit consent
- Web scraping for AI training datasets must exclude biometric/sensitive data without legal basis
- AI companies outside the EU face GDPR enforcement under extraterritorial provisions (Art 3(2))
- AI biometric processing (face recognition, emotion detection, gait analysis) falls under Art 9 strict regime
- Multiple coordinated EU DPA enforcement against a single AI company demonstrates regulatory convergence

GDPRHub Facts Summary:
The controller operates a facial recognition tool (the tool) to identify data subjects using pictures and video's posted online (online content). The controller is established in the United States and has no establishment in the European Union (EU), but processes personal data of EU data subjects. Specifically, it collects online content in which faces appear, including faces of minors. The tool indexes freely accessible web pages and social media platforms. After the indexing, the tool extracts all images with faces of data subjects. Based on these images, the tool calculates a mathematical hash for each data subject, which is in turn based on a unique biometric template of the face in the picture. The mathematical hash is used to make data subjects searchable in the database. The controller sells access to its database to third parties. These third parties can upload a picture of a face to start a search in order to identify data subject, after which the tool creates a mathematical hash for this uploaded picture. This new hash is compared with existing hashes in the database. When the hashes are similar, the tool collects all the images with the same hash, including a reference to the original source of each picture. This process makes it possible to identify data subjects. In its privacy policy, the controller stated that data subjects could only exercise their right of access twice a year. The controller did not mention a retention period for the personal data. The DPA re

GDPRHub Holding Summary:
GDPR applicable? (Article 3(2) GDPR) The DPA held that the GDPR was applicable pursuant ofArticle 3(2) GDPR. Because the controller was not established in the EU, the DPA stated that it was necessary to determine two things: (1) whether the controllerprocessed personal datarelating to data subjects in EU territory and (2) if this processing waslinked to the monitoring of the behaviourof those individuals (recital 24 andGuidelines 3/2018). (1) The DPA held that the controller collected three sorts of personal data according to its privacy policy. It determined that the controller collected publicly accessiblephotographson the internet,information extractedfrom these photographs (such as geolocation data) andinformation from the facial appearanceof data subjects in these photographs. The DPA referred to CJEU case law, stating that the image of the individual photographed or filmed constitutes personal data when the individual can be recognised (see CJEU 11 December 2014, Rynes, C-212/13, point 22 and CJEU, 14 February 2019, F.K., C-345/17). The DPA additionally determined that the controller also processed biometric data (Article 4(1)(14) GDRP)and confirmed that the collection of pictures also concerned data subjects in the EU. (2) Secondly, the DPA held that the processing of the controller waslinked tothemonitoringof thebehaviourof data subjects(Article 3(2)(b) GDPR). The DPA stated that the processingmerely had to be ‘related’ to the monitoring. It was not necessary that monitoring of behaviour was the primary purpose of the processing. The DPA stated that monitoring could also include profiling (Article 4(1)(4) GDPRand recital 24). The DPA held that the search result associated with a photograph was abehavioural profileof the data subject because it contained numerous pieces of information about data subjects or allowed access to this information. The DPA stated that the controller created such behavioural profiles using all its collected pictures of data subjects

On 15 June 2023, the French DPA (CNIL) fined the online advertising company Criteo - the controller - €40,000,000. The DPA’s decision followed complaints lodged by the NGOs Privacy International and None of Your Business (noyb). Criteo used a behavioural targeting approach that tracked data subjects’ online activities to display personalised advertising. By collecting browsing data through its tracking tool (the cookie "Criteo") Criteo analysed data subjects’ browsing habits to determine the most relevant ads for each data subject. Online advertising companies participated then in real-time bidding and displayed personalised ads if they won the bid.

The DPA discovered instances in which the controller’s tracker was used by several of the controller's commercial partners without data subjects’ consent. According to the DPA, obtaining consent from Internet users for the processing of data concerns both Criteo and its commercial partners pursuant to Article 7 GDPR. name: Google/CNIL Cookies
authority: Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL), France
target: Google LLC and Google Ireland Ltd
fine_category: French Data Protection Act / ePrivacy Directive
facts: The CNIL found that google.fr and youtube.com deposited advertising cookies automatically when users visited the sites, before any consent action. The cookie banner offered an easily accessible 'I Accept' button but required multiple clicks to refuse cookies. The CNIL determined that this asymmetric design did not provide a genuine choice and therefore consent was not freely given.
key_findings: Advertising cookies were deposited before the user expressed any preference — a direct violation
The 'reject' option required significantly more clicks than the 'accept' option — consent was not freely given
An equivalent one-click reject mechanism must be provided alongside the accept button
The CNIL has jurisdiction over cookie violations by non-EU entities under ePrivacy rules (not limited by GDPR one-stop-shop)
The fine targeted both the US parent (Google LLC) and the Irish subsidiary
corrective_measures: Provide French users with an equally easy mechanism to refuse cookies as to accept them
Stop depositing cookies before user consent is obtained
Daily penalty of EUR 100,000 for non-compliance (later lifted after compliance)

Authority: Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL), France
Target: Google LLC and Google Ireland Ltd
Decision Date: 2021-12-31
Fine Amount: EUR 150,000,000 (Google LLC: EUR 90M; Google Ireland: EUR 60M — later reduced on appeal)
Fine Category: French Data Protection Act / ePrivacy Directive

Violations:
- French Data Protection Act Article 82 (implementing ePrivacy Directive Art 5(3)) — cookies deposited without valid consent
- Failure to provide equivalent one-click accept/one-click reject mechanism

Facts:
The CNIL found that google.fr and youtube.com deposited advertising cookies automatically when users visited the sites, before any consent action. The cookie banner offered an easily accessible 'I Accept' button but required multiple clicks to refuse cookies. The CNIL determined that this asymmetric design did not provide a genuine choice and therefore consent was not freely given.

Key Findings:
1. Advertising cookies were deposited before the user expressed any preference — a direct violation
2. The 'reject' option required significantly more clicks than the 'accept' option — consent was not freely given
3. An equivalent one-click reject mechanism must be provided alongside the accept button
4. The CNIL has jurisdiction over cookie violations by non-EU entities under ePrivacy rules (not limited by GDPR one-stop-shop)
5. The fine targeted both the US parent (Google LLC) and the Irish subsidiary

Corrective Measures:
- Provide French users with an equally easy mechanism to refuse cookies as to accept them
- Stop depositing cookies before user consent is obtained
- Daily penalty of EUR 100,000 for non-compliance (later lifted after compliance)

- AI analytics and tracking cookies require valid prior consent — no pre-loading before user choice
- AI-powered cookie consent banners (CMPs) must implement symmetric accept/reject UX

name: H&M Employee Surveillance
authority: Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (HmbBfDI), Germany
target: H&M Hennes & Mauritz Online Shop AB & Co. KG
facts: H&M's service centre in Nuremberg conducted systematic and extensive surveillance of employees from at least 2014 to 2019. After employees returned from leave or sick days, their supervisors conducted 'return-to-work' meetings collecting detailed personal information about health conditions, family problems, religious beliefs, and holiday experiences. This data was stored in a comprehensive digital profile system accessible to approximately 50 managers. A technical error in October 2019 briefly made the data accessible to all employees, leading to discovery.

Systematic 'return-to-work' interviews were designed to extract private information
Data was stored for years in an easily searchable digital system without any legal basis
Special category data (Art 9) including health and religious information was processed unlawfully
The data was used to make employment decisions (performance reviews, task assignments)
Approximately 50 managers had access to the employee profiles
corrective_measures: Delete all unlawfully collected employee data
Implement comprehensive data protection compliance programme
H&M also paid compensation to affected employees (total c. EUR 35M)

AI workplace surveillance tools must respect data minimisation — no collection of health, religious, or family data
AI HR analytics using employee personal data for decision-making requires strict legal basis assessment
AI profiling of employees (e.g., attrition prediction, performance scoring) must not process sensitive data unlawfully

Authority: Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (HmbBfDI), Germany
Target: H&M Hennes & Mauritz Online Shop AB & Co. KG
Decision Date: 2020-10-01
Fine Amount: EUR 35,258,707
Fine Category: GDPR Tier 2 (Art 83(5))

Violations:
- GDPR Article 5(1)(a)(b)(c) — violation of lawfulness, purpose limitation, and data minimisation
- GDPR Article 6(1) — no valid legal basis for extensive employee monitoring
- GDPR Article 9 — unlawful processing of special categories of data (health, religion)

Facts:
H&M's service centre in Nuremberg conducted systematic and extensive surveillance of employees from at least 2014 to 2019. After employees returned from leave or sick days, their supervisors conducted 'return-to-work' meetings collecting detailed personal information about health conditions, family problems, religious beliefs, and holiday experiences. This data was stored in a comprehensive digital profile system accessible to approximately 50 managers. A technical error in October 2019 briefly made the data accessible to all employees, leading to discovery.

Key Findings:
1. Extensive personal profiling of employees including health data, family circumstances, religious beliefs
2. Systematic 'return-to-work' interviews were designed to extract private information
3. Data was stored for years in an easily searchable digital system without any legal basis
4. Special category data (Art 9) including health and religious information was processed unlawfully
5. The data was used to make employment decisions (performance reviews, task assignments)
6. Approximately 50 managers had access to the employee profiles

Corrective Measures:
- Delete all unlawfully collected employee data
- Implement comprehensive data protection compliance programme
- H&M also paid compensation to affected employees (total c. EUR 35M)

Appeal Status: No appeal — H&M accepted the fine and cooperated

AI Relevance:

GDPRHub Facts Summary:
H&M with seat in Hamburg operates a service center in Nuremberg. Since at least 2014, issues concerning the private life of employees have been comprehensively recorded and stored. E.g. after absence due to illness or because of vacation, the respective teamleader conducted a "Welcome Back Talk". Detailed information, e.g. information on the symptoms of illness and diagnoses of the employees, has been noted and stored. Moreover,  some supervisors also used information that they heard by accident, for example about family problems and religious beliefs in order to store them on the network drive, which could be accessed by up to 50 managers of the company. This network drive was used to evaluate the performance of the employees and to make employment decisions. This data collection became public due to a technical configuration error in October 2019. The data stored on the network drive could be seen company-wide for hours.

GDPRHub Holding Summary:
H&M is fined in the amount of EUR 35 258 708 for processing data concerning the private life of employees, making them available to up to 50 managers and making employment related decisions on these data. Therefore, H&M has to introduce corrective measures, provide employees with damages and an apology.

name: Marriott Data Breach
facts: Marriott's Starwood guest reservation database was compromised in 2014 (before Marriott's acquisition of Starwood) and remained undetected until September 2018. Approximately 339 million guest records were exposed globally, including 30 million EEA residents' records. Exposed data included names, email addresses, phone numbers, passport numbers, dates of birth, and encrypted payment card details. Marriott failed to conduct adequate due diligence on Starwood's IT systems during the acquisition.
key_findings: The breach originated from Starwood's systems compromised in 2014 — four years before detection
Marriott failed to conduct adequate IT security due diligence during the Starwood acquisition

GDPRHub Facts Summary:
Starwood Hotels and Resorts Worldwide Inc’s (“Starwood”) IT system were first compromised by unknown attackers in 2014. Therefore, between 2014 and 2018, the attackers  had access to Starwood’s systems through use of Remote Access Trojan malware, and kept extracting Starwood databases. Marriott became aware of potential attacks following an alert from a system applied to one of its most confidential databases on September 2018. After that Marriot found malware installed and proof that databases had been extracted over the years, so they promptly notified both the ICO and relevant data subjects of the breach. The ICO found that the attackers had obtained unencrypted personal data of the likes of: passport numbers, identifying information of the costumers such as name, date of birth and gender, plus credit card details in encrypted form.

GDPRHub Holding Summary:
Although the ICO and the relevant victims were notified promptly of the breach, the ICO found that  there were many failures in placing the technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data in Marriott’s system as required under Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR. Marriott’s shortcomings, as outlined by the ICO, were the following: insufficient monitoring of privileged accounts and their user activity, insufficient monitoring of databases, poor control of critical systems and systems that have access to large amounts of personal data, and the fact that only certain type of sensitive data was encrypted (e.g. credit card numbers) but not all (e.g. many passport numbers). The ICO fined Marriott in line ofArticle 83 GDPRbut also took into account mitigating factors such as the efforts that Marriott made to inform and help the victims of the breach, the $19 million investment it made on security the following year and the financial impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic, lowering the final amount of the fine from £24 million to £18.4 million.

Meta Ireland had been transferring personal data to the U.S. despite the lack of a valid adequacy decision underArticle 45 GDPR(as both “safe harbor” and its successor “privacy shield” were invalidated by the CJEU in Schrems I and II). While negotiation of a new adequacy decision for EU-U.S. data transfers are ongoing, Meta Ireland claimed to have undertaken data transfers on the basis of standard contractual clauses adopted by the Commission underArticle 46(2)(c) GDPReven before the CJEU passed the Schrems II decision.

First, the Irish DPA ascertained whether US law guaranteed an essentially equivalent level of protection of data protection rights in light of Schrems II. This was excluded by the supervisory authority, especially due to the lack of effective judicial remedies against the violation of data subjects’ fundamental rights by U.S. intelligence agencies and due to the lack of limitations imposed on the latters’ investigation powers. The latest developments in U.S. law (which are supposed to ensure a higher level of protection for data transferred to the U.S.) were deemed insufficient by the Irish DPA, especially since some of the promised reforms have not yet been implemented. Second, the Irish DPA found that Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) pursuant toArticle 46(2)(c) GDPRinvoked by Meta Ireland could not compensate for the lack of an equivalent level of data protection. In particular, SCCs did not (and could not) address the activity of U.S. intelligence agencies or the lack of judicial remedies against such activity. Third, the supervisory authority considered whether Meta Ireland implemented sufficient supplementary measures that would, in addition to SSCs, ensure an equivalent level of data protection. Finally, Meta Ireland could not rely on derogations underArticle 49 GDPR, as derogations to fundamental rights enshrined in the European Charter of Fundamental Rights shall be interpreted strictly. In this case, the Irish DPA found (following the CJEU in Schrems I and II) that U.S. law interfered with the essence of Europeans’ fundamental rights and therefore did not pass the test set out in Article 52 of the Charter. GDPRHub Facts Summary:
On the 20 August 2018, the French non-profit organisation “La Quadrature du Net” filed a complaint against LinkedIn for intransparent data processing. The complaint had initially been made to the French DPA (CNIL) and was later taken over by the Irish DPA (DPC) as the lead supervisory authority for LinkedIn. The inquiry analysed LinkedIn’s processing of personal data for the purposes of behavioural analysis and targeted advertising to its users. It focussed on the obligation to provide information to data subjects and whether LinkedIn could rely on a legal basis for under Article 6 GDPR for this processing.

GDPRHub Holding Summary:
In a press realease, the DPC highlighted that LinkedIn had breached the overarching principles of fairness and transparency (Article 5(1)(a) GDPR) all throughout the course of the processing. The inquiry found that none of the legal basis invoked by LinkedIn justified the data processing at hand. Specifically, the consent of the LinkedIn users to this processing had not been freely given, sufficiently informed, specific or unambiguous. Further, LinkedIn’s legitimate interests were overridden by the interests and fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects and LinkedIn could not rely on contractual necessity for the processing. In addition, the inquiry showed that the information provided to data subjects by LinkedIn regarding the lawful basis it claimed to rely on, namelyArticle 6(1)(a), 6(1)(b) and 6(1)(f) GDPRwas insufficient. The DPC held that LinkedIn could not rely on consent underArticle 6(1)(a) GDPR, legitimate interests underArticle 6(1)(f) GDPRnor contractual necessity underArticle 6(1)(b) GDPRfor its processing. In addition toArticle 5(1)(a) GDPR, the DPC held that the information provided to data subjects violated Articles13(1)(c)and14(1)(c) GDPR. Made up of three administrative fines, the DPC fined LinkedIn with a total of €310,000,000 for infringements ofArticles 5(1)(a),6(1)(a),6(1)(f),6(1)(b),13(1)(c)and14(1)(c) GDPR. In addition to the fine, the DPC issued a reprimand underArticle 58(2)(b) GDPRand ordered LinkedIn to bring its processing into compliance as perArticle 58(2)(d) GDPR.

Authority: Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten (IMY), Sweden
Target: Spotify AB
Decision Date: 2023-06-13
Fine Amount: EUR 5,000,000 (SEK 58,000,000)
Fine Category: GDPR Tier 1 (Art 83(4))

Violations:
- GDPR Article 15 — failure to provide adequately clear access to personal data
- GDPR Article 12 — information provided was not transparent, intelligible or easily accessible

Facts:
The Swedish DPA (IMY) investigated Spotify following complaints from data subjects (co-ordinated by noyb) about the quality of responses to data subject access requests. Spotify provided data subjects with a downloadable data package, but the IMY found that it was not sufficiently clear how the different data categories related to the information requirements under Article 15 GDPR. Spotify's explanations of purposes and retention periods were unclear.

Key Findings:
1. Spotify's data download package did not clearly map to the mandatory information under Article 15 GDPR
2. Purposes of processing were described too vaguely in access request responses
3. Retention periods were not adequately specified for different data categories
4. Providing raw data without clear context/explanation is insufficient to satisfy Art 15
5. The format of access responses must be intelligible and meaningful to the average data subject

Corrective Measures:
- Restructure access request responses to clearly respond to each element of Article 15
- Provide clear explanations of purposes and retention periods per data category

Appeal Status: Fine upheld (2024)

AI Relevance:
- AI music recommendation engines must provide clear, structured responses to access requests about profiling data
- AI systems processing personal data must be able to generate meaningful Art 15 access responses — not just raw data dumps
- AI-derived inferences and profiles are personal data subject to access rights
- AI services must provide transparency about how AI-generated categories and preferences relate to personal data collected

Authority: Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC)
Target: TikTok Technology Ltd
Decision Date: 2023-09-01
Fine Amount: EUR 345,000,000
Fine Category: GDPR Tier 2 (Art 83(5))

Violations:
- GDPR Article 5(1)(a) — violation of fairness principle (dark patterns for children)
- GDPR Article 5(1)(c) — violation of data minimisation for children's data
- GDPR Article 5(1)(f) — violation of integrity and confidentiality
- GDPR Article 12-13 — insufficient transparency for children
- GDPR Article 24 — inadequate measures for child protection
- GDPR Article 25 — failure to implement privacy by design and by default for children

Facts:
The DPC investigated TikTok's processing of children's (aged 13-17) personal data following requests from Dutch and French DPAs. TikTok set children's accounts to 'public' by default, used 'dark patterns' to nudge minors towards less private settings, failed to implement adequate age verification, and did not provide age-appropriate transparency information. The EDPB issued a binding decision under Art 65(1)(a) requiring the DPC to find additional violations regarding dark patterns and the fairness principle.

Key Findings:
1. Children's TikTok accounts were set to 'public' by default — violating privacy by design and by default
2. TikTok used 'dark patterns' to nudge children towards accepting less private settings ('Skip' vs 'Go Private')
3. The EDPB found violations of the FAIRNESS principle (Art 5(1)(a)) — a novel enforcement development
4. Age verification mechanisms (age gate) were easily circumvented
5. The EDPB highlighted that the principle of data protection by design requires 'state of the art' age verification
6. Transparency information was not adapted to be understandable by children

Corrective Measures:
- Bring processing into compliance with GDPR requirements for children's data
- Implement privacy-by-default settings for all child accounts
- Eliminate dark patterns from the consent/settings interfaces for minors

Appeal Status: Under appeal (2024)

AI Relevance:
- AI recommendation algorithms for minors must implement privacy-by-default principles
- AI-powered 'engagement optimisation' for children constitutes dark patterns when it undermines privacy choices
- AI age verification systems represent 'state of the art' measures that platforms may be required to implement
- AI content curation for children must respect data minimisation — no collecting unnecessary behavioural data
- AI UX design optimising for data collection from children is a GDPR violation (fairness + dark patterns)

Authority: Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), Netherlands
Target: Uber Technologies Inc. and Uber B.V.
Decision Date: 2024-08-26
Fine Amount: EUR 290,000,000
Fine Category: GDPR Tier 2 (Art 83(5))

Violations:
- GDPR Article 44 — unlawful international transfer of personal data
- GDPR Chapter V — transfers without appropriate safeguards

Facts:
The Dutch DPA (AP), acting as Lead Supervisory Authority, found that Uber transferred personal data of European drivers to the US for over two years without a valid transfer mechanism. Following the Schrems II judgment, Uber discontinued use of SCCs but then failed to implement an alternative valid transfer mechanism for a prolonged period. The case was initiated following mass complaints filed by French taxi drivers via the French human rights organisation Ligue des Droits de l'Homme, referred to the Dutch DPA as Lead Supervisory Authority.

Key Findings:
1. Uber transferred EU driver data to US servers for over two years without any valid transfer mechanism
2. After Schrems II invalidated the Privacy Shield, Uber failed to rapidly implement alternative safeguards
3. Driver data included highly sensitive information: location tracking, identity documents, earnings data
4. The prolonged duration of non-compliance (2+ years) was an aggravating factor
5. The Dutch DPA acted as Lead Supervisory Authority — one-stop-shop mechanism applied
6. Third-highest GDPR fine ever at time of issuance

Corrective Measures:
- Bring all data transfers to the US into compliance with GDPR Chapter V
- Implement valid transfer mechanisms compliant with Schrems II requirements

Appeal Status: Under appeal (2024). Uber claims EU-US Data Privacy Framework now covers its transfers.

AI Relevance:
- AI ride-hailing algorithms processing EU driver/rider location data in US data centres face same transfer restrictions
- AI pricing algorithms (surge pricing) using EU personal data must comply with Chapter V transfer rules
- AI driver monitoring and scoring systems transmitting EU data to US must have valid transfer mechanisms
- Gig economy AI platforms (Uber, Lyft, DoorDash) face high exposure for cross-border data transfer violations

On the applicability ofArticle 3 GDPRand Chapter V The DPA noted that the rationale behind Chapter V of the GDPR on data transfer was complementary to the rationale ofArticle 3 GDPRon the territorial scope, as it prevents the denial, undermining or circumvention of data protection under EU law. The DPA noted that although the GDPR applies to all processing operations underArticle 3 GDPR, the application of the GDPR outside the EEA territory did not provide the same protection. Therefore, the provisions in Chapter V contain mechanisms, which counterbalance the difficulty of enforcing obligations under EU law against parties in third countries. The DPA held that any other interpretation of these mechanisms would result in a weakening of the protection offered within the Union, which is not consistent with the standard required by the CJEU (seeC-40/17 - Fashion ID). Thus, the controllers' argument that Chapter V did not apply whenArticle 3 GDPRapplies, would be contrary to the rationale behind Chapter V in the GDPR. The DPA also stated that nowhere in the GDPR was stated thatArticle 3 GDPRtook precedence over Chapter V.
